The post Review: Ritual Zero Proof Canned Cocktails, Complete Lineup appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Ritual, well known for its non-alcoholic spirit alternatives, recently launched a ready-to-drink non-alc collection, canned cocktails available in three classic flavors. We tried them all.

Ritual Zero Proof G&T – A self-explanatory non-alc gin and tonic, this is an easygoing experience that is heavy with lime, almost overblown at times. Piney juniper is vaguely hinted at, but at least present in some level. Turns out however that the bitterness of the tonic is very mild, and frankly it could use a lot more of it in order to balance out the sour-sweet lime notes. It’s not a bad rendition of a gin and tonic, but the last thing I would have expected to wish for when tasting this spirit has nothing to do with the hard part of the equation (the non-alcoholic gin) and everything to do with the tonic. That said, it’s awfully easy-drinking and can fool you at least partway into thinking it’s the real thing. A-

Ritual Zero Proof Spritz – Bright orange in color and bright orange in flavor, this initially comes across closer to an orange soda than a proper spritz, though mercifully some bitterness manages to temper the fruit later in the game. As with the G&T, there’s still not enough of of that bittering element, and the experience could definitely withstand a bolder, more aggressive quinine quality to make it feel more grown-up. The fizz is moderated but appropriate, and the finish offers a little lime as an orangey complement, though the conclusion sweetens up further and evokes notes of tangerine. A-

Ritual Zero Proof Margarita – A lemon-lime attack gives this concoction a soda-like quality to start, but let it sit on the tongue for a bit and a curious herbal-earthy quality comes into focus. From here the expression finds some salinity and a hint of peppery heat, the finish especially evoking a healthy pinch of salt. It’s never too sweet, letting citrus do most of the talking throughout the sip. While you won’t mistake this for an authentic margarita, it is a pleasant N/A alternative that at least scratches that sweet-and-sour itch enough to work alongside a serving of chips and salsa. B+

each $14 per four-pack of 12 oz cans

title: Review: 1792 Straight Rye
summary:
After a few years of sleepiness, Sazerac’s 1792 brand has finally started to get some much-needed and much-deserved attention again. It started with last year’s 1792 Cognac Cask Finish Bourbon and it continues in 2026 with the release of a 15-year-old expression and this whiskey, the first-ever straight rye expression from the brand and a new…

The post Review: 1792 Straight Rye appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
After a few years of sleepiness, Sazerac’s 1792 brand has finally started to get some much-needed and much-deserved attention again. It started with last year’s 1792 Cognac Cask Finish Bourbon and it continues in 2026 with the release of a 15-year-old expression and this whiskey, the first-ever straight rye expression from the brand and a new part of the permanent portfolio.

It’s distilled at the Barton 1792 distillery by Master Distiller Ross Cornelissen using the same yeast 1792 uses for its bourbon, though the grains used in the mash are sourced globally from Canada, Europe, and the northern United States. Sazerac, as is tradition, does not disclose the official mashbill for the whiskey, nor does this bottling include an age statement.

Let’s taste.

1792 Straight Rye Review

The whiskey is rye-forward on the nose without being aggressive; there’s clearly plenty of corn in the mash here (and perhaps an assist from that bourbon yeast) to give it an appropriate tempering. Sweet corn, caramel, and vanilla notes are all evident yet kept in check by ample greenery and spice. The rye isn’t shy about muscling its way to the forefront of the nose, especially given some time in glass. Alongside notes of cut grass and ground black pepper, the whiskey makes room for touches of menthol, bay leaf, and a hint of anise.

The palate is chewy and plenty racy at 50% abv, again carefully toeing the line between its pastoral greenery and its sweeter, nuttier elements. Peppery bay leaf elements are the most dominant element, particularly at full strength, hinting at jalapeno as the whiskey’s attack fades just a bit. Baked apples and a sweetened almond note are insistent, really honing in on that chewy quality, though it’s not a flavor you typically find in rye. Notes of dark chocolate, laced with cinnamon, give the finish a pop and help to lift the whiskey out of what can sometimes offer a slightly doughy consistency.

On its own I found this experience to have waves of brilliance amidst an otherwise fairly straightforward trajectory. It won’t wow the single barrel crowd, but at 40 bucks a bottle and 100 proof, this is an outstanding mixing rye that your Sazerac should adore.

100 proof.

B+/ $40

summary:

The post Review: 2023 The Prisoner Grail Stags Leap District appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The Prisoner got its start by Dave Phinney in 2000 as a fairly simple red blend, but somehow the brand promptly exploded in popularity, becoming both a cult and mainstream favorite while adding all manner of expressions as well as spin-off labels, many of which we’ve covered.

Now, under the eye of winemaker Todd Ricard, the brand is reaching higher than ever with The Prisoner Grail, a cab-heavy blend that aims for its highest price point at $200 a bottle. The 2023 bottling is a blend of 72% cabernet sauvignon, 20% syrah, and 8% cabernet franc, crafted from three blocks from the prized Wappo Hill Vineyard in the Napa Valley. Aging was undertaken for 18 months, 60% in new French oak.

While I will complain that the wax seal is one of the most difficult I’ve ever encountered to remove, I’ll move on quickly to dig into the wine, which stands as one of the finest (almost) cabernets you’ll likely find on the market today.

The wine explodes out of the gate with a rush of currants and blackberry, along with some brighter, sweeter blueberry notes. The wine is not shy about its density — at 15.5% abv it approaches dessert wine booziness — but it keeps overt sweetness in check thanks its silky tannins and gentle notes of graphite, tobacco, and a pinch of white pepper. Layers of chocolate unfold from there, again not overly sugary, with vanilla and baking spice notes building on the finish. The fade-out sees plenty of lingering berry fruit, touched with some sweeter tobacco elements and lingering licorice notes.

Powerful stuff.

A / $200

title: Review: Tamdhu 21 Years Old
summary:

As with the rest of the lineup, this 21 year old expression is aged entirely in oloroso sherry casks, both American and European oak, features natural color, and has no chill-filtration. Tamdhu…

The post Review: Tamdhu 21 Years Old appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The oldest whisky in the Tamdhu core range is this 21 year old expression, complementing its 18, 15, and 12 year old offerings.

As with the rest of the lineup, this 21 year old expression is aged entirely in oloroso sherry casks, both American and European oak, features natural color, and has no chill-filtration.

Tamdhu 21 Years Old Review

21 years of sherry cask aging is a long time, and Tamdhu 21 wears that time on its sleeve. On the nose, it’s really all you can smell, a very austere olfactory punch that features glazed nuts, reduced maple syrup, and wet furniture varnish. Aromatic? You bet, but the intensity is off the charts, that dense aroma of aged citrus peels, pipe tobacco, and a massive pinch of allspice fill the airway completely. Peppery and sweet and so very well aged all at once, it’s hard to shake once the aromatics take hold.

The palate continues the theme — sharp, citrusy, nutty, and leathery all at once. Sherried single malt enthusiasts will find this all too familiar, that Spanish spice verging on an almost hoary rancio character as it sits on the tongue. There’s so much fruit and baking spice here, however, that Tamdhu 21 never falls back into the leatherworker’s shop, treading water just above the line that could suck it into the back room of a Turkish rug shop, closed off in the flavors of antiquity. I liked it best with a healthy splash of water, which brings out the cookie-like notes of chocolate and caramel that you’ll find in some of the 18 year old Tamdhu expression — both particularly evident on the lengthy and citrus-forward finish.

95 proof.

A- / $400

title: Review: Fanttik Cafein 11 Portable Coffee Maker
summary:
Folks who need their caffeine fix no matter what the circumstances are can sometimes find themselves in dire straits. If you’re on the road, in the woods, or simply far from a Starbucks, what’s a java junkie to do? Fanttik’s Cafein 11 proffers a solution: This is a portable coffee-brewing machine that needs only two…

The post Review: Fanttik Cafein 11 Portable Coffee Maker appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Folks who need their caffeine fix no matter what the circumstances are can sometimes find themselves in dire straits. If you’re on the road, in the woods, or simply far from a Starbucks, what’s a java junkie to do?

Fanttik’s Cafein 11 proffers a solution: This is a portable coffee-brewing machine that needs only two ingredients: Coffee (or a Nespresso-like coffee pod) and water. Regular water, not boiling. Armed with a couple of simple ingredients and a fully charged battery, the Cafein lets you produce 5 to 8 (tiny) cups of coffee while otherwise fully disconnected from the grid, no strings attached.

Sound too good to be true? I put the device to the test to see if the reality measured up to the promises, and I’m mostly happy to say that yes, it did. While there’s a bit of a learning curve (and lots of pieces to navigate), the Cafein 11 is ultimately fairly easy to use. Measure ground coffee into the tiny filter basket, screw it into the main chassis, and add water to the other side. A built-in insulated cup captures the coffee that comes out the bottom, in a process that takes about 2 minutes.

The completed brew tastes great — this unit can heat water to 198 degrees and push 20 bars of pressure, which helps to create a modest crema on top of the beverage. I couldn’t really tell any difference between the quality of the coffee the Cafein 11 produced vs. a Nespresso.

Except for one thing: The amount of coffee the Cafein 11 produces is tiny, just 80ml at most, or less than 3 ounces of brewed coffee. It’s a tiny amount even in the miniature serving cup that Fanttik provides, so small that it looks like something went wrong. Nope, that’s just how much — or how little — coffee it can produce.

There are surely reasons for this: The unit is designed to be kept small, and heating up water requires a lot of energy. The more coffee you make, the bigger the battery would need to be, which would cause this lose its portability. Yes, you can always make more than one cup, but that’s not easy with the Cafein, either: The filter basket gets very hot and needs to cool down (and be cleaned out) before being used again. Cleanup isn’t difficult, but it’s time consuming, much like the setup process is. You’ll need access to running water to do a proper cleanup job of tidying up the 6 components you’re left with at the end of a single coffee run.

Those issues aside, I had fun playing with the Cafein 11 at home, and can — maybe — see a use for a device like this on a camping trip or a boat day. The quantity issue remains the thorniest of its few concerns, though, and there’s no easy way to get around it — except by maybe forcing yourself to make do with a demitasse instead of the Venti you’re used to.

B / $140 [BUY IT NOW FROM AMAZON]

A pocho is slang for a Mexican who grew up in…

The post Review: Pocho Fino Tequilas, Complete Lineup appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Gabriel “Flully” Iglesias is a widely enjoyed stand-up comedian, often using his Hispanic ancestry as part of his routines. Now the man is a tequila magnate, launching his own brand of blanco and flavored offerings. “Pocho Fino” is a tongue-in-cheek reference perhaps to Iglesias himself. A pocho is slang for a Mexican who grew up in the U.S., presumably losing his Latino heritage along the way, while fino means refined. Essentially: “Fancy Mexican immigrant.”

Let’s try the full lineup.

NOM 1437.

Pocho Fino Blanco Tequila Review

Rustic and a little dirty on the nose, this presents with aromas of mushroom and hemp rope, undercut with solvent. There’s a hint of fruit somewhere underneath all that, but the payoff from spending half an hour nosing this tequila to find it is decidedly minimal. The palate doesn’t offer much beyond all that, though the leathery notes of underbrush are at least sweetened up enough to temper the tequila’s aggressively savory elements. Notes of coconut nectar and almond syrup are evident, but fleeting, as the finish falls back on its industrial qualities. 80 proof. C- / $27

Pocho Fino Mexican Candy Tequila Review

Mexican candy is a broad (and often scary) category, but officially the flavor selection here is described as “candied watermelon meets fresh lime and jalapeño that is infused in the blanco tequila.” (The label does not describe the flavors as either natural or artificial.) As I had suspected, a healthy dose of flavoring does wonders for masking the funk of the blanco tequila, and the fruit pans out better than any actual Mexican candy I’ve ever tasted. Watermelon and lime effectively work as a boozy Jolly Rancher, though jalapeno notes are fleeting at best. Nuanced, no, but quaffable. 70 proof. B / $16

Pocho Fino Grilled Pineapple Tequila Review

More obvious in construction, with (natural) caramelized pineapple the flavoring note. This one’s also tinged slightly yellow in color. The results are very sweet and candylike — and so sugary it’s a little hard to describe. Brown sugar sweetness overwhelms the pineapple character, coming across like a hotel bar happy hour special made out of leftover liqueurs and rail tequila. The herbal tequila flavor does come through a bit more clearly here than on the wholly neutral Mexican Candy expression, but that’s not an overwhelmingly positive thing, as it exhibits the same industrial tendencies of the blanco, only masked by the intense flavoring agents. Definitely something I could handle only in small quantities. 70 proof. C / $16

title: Review: Maison Wessman Hot Blood Wines, 2026 Releases
summary:
We recently reviewed the red and white Raven wines from Maison Wessman, which were made in collaboration with musician JJ Julius Son, the frontman for the band Kaleo. Now we swing back to try the other two wines that Wessman and JJ Julius Son produced together, the Hot Blood red and white. An interesting aspect…

The post Review: Maison Wessman Hot Blood Wines, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We recently reviewed the red and white Raven wines from Maison Wessman, which were made in collaboration with musician JJ Julius Son, the frontman for the band Kaleo. Now we swing back to try the other two wines that Wessman and JJ Julius Son produced together, the Hot Blood red and white. An interesting aspect of the two pairs of wines is that they showcase very similar grapes but from different appellations in France and in the case of the red wine, slightly different percentages of grapes. I’ll include details of each in their respective descriptions. Let’s give them a try.

2022 Hot Blood Merlot & Cabernet Sauvignon – 70% Merlot, 20% Cabernet Sauvignon, 10% Malbec. In contrast to the Raven red, this wine is Merlot heavy and includes some Malbec, with the grapes grown in Bergerac, France. On both the nose and palate, this intriguing Bordeaux blend showcases deep, fruity notes of Bing cherry, plum, blackberry, and raspberry along with herbal notes of black pepper, sage, and thyme, including a bit of menthol. It is fairly complex with the individual notes standing out, though they also play together nicely. There’s good structure here with high acidity and gentle tannins that provide a nice drying finish as the menthol note slowly fades away. The herbal note might be the key to this wine, and those who appreciate it will really enjoy it. I think it would pair brilliantly with lamb with mint sauce or mint jelly. A- / $17

2023 Hot Blood Chardonnay – Like White Raven, Hot Blood is 100% Chardonnay, but drawn from the Pays d’Oc region of Languedoc. This wine also differs from the former in that it was not aged in oak but in stainless steel, where it rested on the lees for an undisclosed amount of time. On the nose, it offers juicy aromas of lemon tart, granny smith apple, and peach. On the palate, it is fruity with lime pith, lemon, peach, and a touch of pineapple. The wine shows high acidity and a touch of minerality, but the finish is a bit short. The acidity is high enough that I recommend enjoying it with food, and in the summer months, I would love to serve it alongside a Caprese salad. B+ / $17

title: Review: Bear Fight Kentucky Reserve Straight Bourbon
summary:
The Bear Fight brand got started with the launch of an elaborately finished American single malt, and recently owner Next Century Spirits has expanded the line to a second bottling, Bear Fight Kentucky Reserve Straight Bourbon, a (sourced) high-rye bourbon that is finished in reposado tequila casks. No age statements or sourcing information, so let’s…

The post Review: Bear Fight Kentucky Reserve Straight Bourbon appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
The Bear Fight brand got started with the launch of an elaborately finished American single malt, and recently owner Next Century Spirits has expanded the line to a second bottling, Bear Fight Kentucky Reserve Straight Bourbon, a (sourced) high-rye bourbon that is finished in reposado tequila casks.

No age statements or sourcing information, so let’s dig right in.

Bear Fight Kentucky Reserve Straight Bourbon Review

Spoiler: You will not miss the tequila finishing here, the whiskey offering a spicy nose that exudes notes of chocolate and cinnamon, then dark brown sugar. There’s plenty of peppery spice visible, to the point where you might ask whether this was some kind of tequila-whiskey blend. Just how “wet” were those finishing barrels, I wonder.

While the nose drips with tequila, the palate is a little more subtle. A little. Here, the doughy-peanutty quality of a rather young bourbon dominates — all the tequila in the world can’t wash that away. The underlying cinnamon and emerging notes of nutmeg and cloves do however complement this nutty attack, creating a dessert-like experience that works well with the chocolate notes present. In fact, without the finishing barrel this would be about as boring a whiskey as you could imagine. The finish is sweet and spicy, without coming across as saccharine or candylike. For a bourbon that’s been manipulated to this degree, that’s a bit of a feat.

As it stands, the price tag alone makes this an attractive buy, but the unique combination of whiskey and tequila works better here than I’ve seen in other iterations of this formula. Definitely not a daily sipper for me, but it’s unique enough to merit some level of consideration, especially for use in a bespoke cocktail.

90 proof.

B+ / $38 [BUY IT NOW FROM FROOTBAT]

title: Review: Wines of Xander Soren, 2026 Releases
summary:
We greatly enjoyed our last go-round with California’s Xander Soren wines, and recently the operation sent a full complement of new releases, spanning all eight of its current offerings on the market — this time including whites and reds (and one rose). Reviews are presented in order of preference. Note that the winery’s entry-level wines…

The post Review: Wines of Xander Soren, 2026 Releases appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
We greatly enjoyed our last go-round with California’s Xander Soren wines, and recently the operation sent a full complement of new releases, spanning all eight of its current offerings on the market — this time including whites and reds (and one rose). Reviews are presented in order of preference.

Note that the winery’s entry-level wines are denoted by a colored label and only the name “Xander,” sans “Soren.”

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Ludeon Central Coast – A supple and seductive wine, this is the pinnacle of Xander Soren’s collection and it immediately shows. Deftly balanced among notes of tart cherry, soothing raspberry, bittersweet chocolate, and orange flower blossoms, this wine weaves back and forth on the palate as it evolves in glass to coax out elements of tea leaf before finishing on a brighter touch of orange peel. Layers of walnut, darker chocolate, and hints of coffee emerge, all melding beautifully into the experience. Impossible to put down, this is American pinot at its finest. A / $195

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Olivet Lane Russian River Valley – The lone RRV pinot in the mix here, I was expecting a dense monster of a wine, in keeping with the region’s typical style. Shocker: This is gentle and approachable and full of exuberance, layered with surprisingly easygoing notes of ripe cherry and strawberry, touched with tea leaf and, later, bay leaf notes. While fairly straightforward, hints of vanilla and a little chocolate force their way into a tart and fruity palate that maintains an acidic brightness from start to finish. Impossible to put down, this wine made me wholly rethink everything about pinot from the Russian River Valley. A / $125

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Sanford & Benedict Sta. Rita Hills – Quite a savory expression of pinot, with a strong tomato leaf note visible up front. This sharper edge finds a complement in notes of cranberry and some extracted cherry elements, hinting at almond as the finish builds. More savory notes of tobacco leaf, bay leaf, and a touch of coffee give the conclusion a brooding character, though a final spritz of orange oil livens things up just so. Consider decanting to accelerate the development process — and pair the wine appropriately. A- / $125

2021 Xander Chardonnay Santa Barbara County – Pouring this wine — Soren’s $75 entry-level bottling — into a glass reveals an initial rush of earth and leather, but time is your friend with this one. Slowly the wine opens up as it warms to showcase evolving layers of coconut and almond nougat, with lemon curd notes offering a powerful undercurrent of tart fruit. I was initially a little put off by the hoarier elements of the experience, but thing changed with surprising speed as the lively underbelly of lemon, lime, and green apple present in the wine shifted into prominence. In short order, the wine came out of its shell and blossomed like a butterfly to reveal an exuberant muse, gently floral but still citrus-forward and palate-cleansing, a perfect pairing for a spicy dinner. A- / $75

2021 Xander Soren Chardonnay Habari Sta. Rita Hills – This single-vineyard chardonnay from the El Jabali Vineyard pours with a surprising austerity, coming across as rather bitter at the start, keeping the drinker at arm’s length as it takes its time to develop. Air and some warmth allow the wine to develop more nuance — gooseberry, pear, and some tart green apple notes all sparring with a distinctively moderated barrel character that comes off with more of an aged melon vibe. (The wine is aged in only 10% new French oak.) The level of acidity here is quite surprising, with saline notes lingering well into the finish and tempering what wood is present. Notes of honeydew inform the fade-out. Above all: Give this wine plenty of time. It’s closed off at the start, but time spent digging into it reveals far more charm than I ever expected. A- / $150

2021 Xander Soren Pinot Noir Yuki Vineyard West Sonoma Coast – Boldly cherry-forward, the expressive fruit here settles down with time to reveal earthier notes, particularly tea leaf and more muted notes of bay leaf, finishing with a chewy, tobacco-like quality. The fade-out is earthier than I expected (or desired), but when paired with a lively meal (I tried mushroom Bolognese) the combination works remarkably well. B+ / $125

2025 Xander Rose of Pinot Noir California Cuvee – I’m not sure what I was expecting with this rose, but the burst of strawberry that hits the senses immediately wasn’t it. Incredibly fruity, bordering on candylike at times, the wine is flush with fruit but also features plenty of brighter elements — lemon peel and salinity — before shifting back to feature some dried floral notes. A touch of almond informs the finish. Certainly crowd-pleasing, but not at all what I though would be in the mix. B+ / $50

2021 Xander Pinot Noir Santa Barbara County – Xander Soren’s entry-level pinot (albeit a $75 wine) strikes with a shocking smokiness, notes of underbrush aflame, dried tea leaves, and cardamom, creating a savory experience that feels more than a little blown out and aggressive. That might not be such a problem if the wine had a powerful body to stand up against the smoky onslaught, but this pinot hits the palate as distinctly thin, pale in color, with a finish that evokes weak tea — touched of course with smoke. Was wildfire an issue with this vintage in Santa Barbara? B- / $75

title: Review: Four Roses Anthology Chapter One: Origin 21 Years Old (2026)
summary:
Jonesing for ultra-ultra-premium whiskey? Four Roses is the latest to have you covered with a unicorn offering, the first in a new luxe series called Anthology. Anthology will be an annually released whiskey, a collection of rarities designed to “explore key chapters in the brand’s 138-year history. The inaugural release, Chapter One: Origin, is a…

The post Review: Four Roses Anthology Chapter One: Origin 21 Years Old (2026) appeared first on Drinkhacker: The Insider's Guide to Good Drinking.
content:
Jonesing for ultra-ultra-premium whiskey? Four Roses is the latest to have you covered with a unicorn offering, the first in a new luxe series called Anthology. Anthology will be an annually released whiskey, a collection of rarities designed to “explore key chapters in the brand’s 138-year history. The inaugural release, Chapter One: Origin, is a 21-year-old OBSF bourbon and the oldest release in Four Roses history.”

Taking that further: “The first chapter is inspired by Four Roses’ founding story, when founder Paul Jones Jr. named the brand after his Southern belle accepted his marriage proposal by wearing a corsage of four red roses to a grand ball in 1888. The release pays tribute to the moment that inspired the brand and the themes of love and connection that continue to define Four Roses today.”

I don’t know who’ll be able to snap up one of the 1200 bottles (mainly at the Four Roses Visitor’s Center), but, well, let’s see how it tastes.

Four Roses Anthology Chapter One: Origin 21 Years Old (2026) Review

The nose promptly showcases the age of this whiskey. Austere and tannic, the rye-forward qualities of OBSF are amplified to the hilt here, bold with cloves and extra-dark chocolate. Time in glass takes this latter note and runs with it, turning coffee-like as it develops in a Glencairn. Gravelly and intense, there’s nothing subtle about the experience, as it wholly connotes the significant density to come.

Intense and quite wine-like on the tongue, the aromatic buildup is paid off immediately. Old and layered with wood, the charry-tarry bourbon unfolds with amazing austerity, evoking tobacco leaf, leather, and tar in quick succession. If there’s fruit left in the barrel, it fully evaporates before it hits the glass: This is 100% savory, though that doesn’t mean it’s without nuance. Elements of walnut (namely shell), black pepper, burnt grass, and lingering creosote all combine to create a, well, appropriately ancient but surprisingly immersive sip. It tastes extremely old, but as a famous Monty Python character might has said, not quite dead yet. The longer it sits in the glass and on the tongue, the more its latent life is revealed. Be patient.

Ultimately, a hint of molasses on the finish gives you the lightest respite from what can be a somewhat overwhelming experience. Maybe that touch of sweetness is all it took to get me to wonder if a second taste lies somewhere in my future. Probably not, alas.

102.6 proof.

A- / $500
